hero.title: Know what you need before you pay for it
hero.subtitle: Website, dashboard, system, SaaS… they sound alike but they solve different problems. In a few minutes you'll know the difference and which one fits your business.

items.text: Most customers look a business up online before they call, visit, or buy.
People judge how serious a business is by its website. No website, or a weak one, makes them doubt.
Most visits now come from phones, so the site must work perfectly on a small screen.
Many customers want to book or order at night or on weekends, when nobody answers the phone. A website takes their request anytime.
In our region almost everyone uses WhatsApp. A website that connects to WhatsApp meets customers where they already are.

types.title: The four types of software, explained with a shop
types.summary: Four kinds of software, four different jobs. Choose by what you need to do: be found, take bookings, run your team, or sell software.
types.intro: Think of your business as a shop. Each type of software is a different part of it.

items.name: Profile website
items.oneLine: Your business's front window on the internet.
items.analogy: The sign and the brochure of your shop, open 24 hours a day.
items.whatItDoes: Shows who you are, your services, your work, and how to reach you (call, WhatsApp, map).
items.examples: A company website, a clinic's information site, a portfolio for a designer or a lawyer.
items.goodFor: Being found on Google, building trust, turning visitors into calls and WhatsApp messages.
items.youManage: Little. Text and photos change sometimes.

items.name: Functional website + dashboard
items.oneLine: A website that does work for you, plus a dashboard where you manage it.
items.analogy: A shop with a reception desk that takes bookings and orders even when you're closed, and an office where you see everything.
items.whatItDoes: Customers book, order, or send requests on the site. You see and manage them in your dashboard, and you edit the site's content yourself.
items.examples: A restaurant with table booking, a clinic with appointments, a company that receives quote requests, a small online store.
items.goodFor: Saving time on calls, not missing customers at night, keeping every request organized in one place.

items.name: Custom business system
items.oneLine: Software for your team, built around the way you work.
items.analogy: The back office and stockroom of your shop, organized exactly your way.
items.whatItDoes: Organizes internal work: customers, stock, staff, tasks, invoices, reports. Mainly used by your team, not the public.
items.examples: A system to follow customers and sales (CRM), inventory for a store, job tracking for a maintenance company, a school's student management.
items.goodFor: Replacing paper, Excel sheets, and scattered WhatsApp groups. Fewer mistakes, clear reports.
items.youManage: Your team uses it every day, with accounts and permissions.
items.effort: Medium to high, depending on how much it does

items.name: SaaS product
items.oneLine: Software that you sell to many businesses for a monthly subscription.
items.analogy: Instead of running one shop, you build a ready "shop system" and rent it to hundreds of shop owners.
items.whatItDoes: Many companies sign up, each with its own account, data, and team, and pay you a subscription.
items.examples: A booking platform for all clinics in a city, an accounting app for small shops, a delivery-management tool for restaurants.
items.goodFor: Building a software business with recurring income.
items.youManage: Customers' accounts, subscriptions and payments, support, and continuous improvement.
items.effort: High. It's a product and a company, not a single project.
items.note: Important: if the software is only for your own business, you don't need a SaaS. You need a custom business system.

rentOrBuild.title: Ready-made tool or your own?
rentOrBuild.summary: Rent what everyone needs. Build only what makes your business different.
rentOrBuild.text: For many needs there are ready-made online tools you rent monthly. They're quick to start. Your own (custom) software costs more at the start, but it fits your exact way of working, carries your brand, and belongs to you.

rent.label: Rent when
rent.text: your need is common, you want to start this week, and the monthly cost stays small.

build.label: Build when
build.text: the tools force you into workarounds, you pay for many subscriptions that don't talk to each other, your way of working is what makes you different, or the subscriptions over a few years would cost more than building.

mix.label: Smart mix
mix.text: Many businesses rent tools for common tasks and build only the part that makes them special.

howBuilt.title: How software is built, in shop terms

items.title: The front (what customers see)
items.text: Pages, buttons, forms. Like the shop floor and window.

items.title: The dashboard (what you see)
items.text: Where you read requests and change content. Like your office.

items.title: The server (the brain)
items.text: Receives each request, checks it, and decides what to do. Like the staff behind the counter.

items.title: The database (the memory)
items.text: Where customers, bookings, and orders are stored safely. Like a well-organized filing cabinet.

items.title: Domain and hosting
items.text: The domain is your address (yourname.com); hosting is the land the shop stands on. Both are renewed yearly or monthly.

items.title: Ongoing care
items.text: Updates, security, backups, and improvements. Like servicing a car so it keeps running.

myths.title: Myths and the truth
myths.summary: Most costly mistakes come from a few wrong ideas. Open each myth to see the truth behind it.

items.myth: A website is paid once and that's it.
items.truth: Building is paid once, but the domain, hosting, updates, and security continue. Plan a small yearly budget.

items.myth: Once it's launched, the work is done.
items.truth: Launch is the start. You learn from visitors, improve, and add what brings more customers.
You don't own your social page, and its reach can change overnight. Your website is yours, builds trust, and works with your social pages and WhatsApp.

items.myth: More features means a better website.
items.truth: Every feature should bring value. Start with what brings customers or saves time, then grow.

items.myth: I need a SaaS for my business.
items.truth: SaaS is software you sell to other businesses. For your own work you usually need a functional website or a custom system.

items.myth: The cheapest offer is the best deal.
items.truth: The real cost includes the customers you lose if the site is slow, confusing, or not trusted. Compare value, not only price.

items.myth: If I build it, customers will come.
items.truth: A website needs to be shared, found on Google, and linked from your social pages and WhatsApp.
Most customers check online before they call or visit, even for local businesses.

items.definition: The computer on the internet where your website lives, always on.
The site adjusts itself to phones, tablets, and computers.
Work that helps your site appear in Google results.
The lock icon in the browser; it protects the data your customers send.
The private page where you manage your site and your requests.
Editing your site's text and photos yourself, without a developer.
The smallest version that delivers real value, launched fast and improved later.
A saved copy of your site and data, in case something goes wrong.
